techniques.name: Data Obfuscation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

techniques.name: Junk Data
techniques.summary: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

techniques.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

techniques.name: Data Compressed
techniques.summary: An adversary may compress data (e.g., sensitive documents) that is collected prior to exfiltration in order to make it portable and minimize the amount of data sent over the network.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password.

techniques.name: LSASS Memory
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

techniques.name: Security Account Manager
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored.

techniques.name: NTDS
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights.

techniques.name: LSA Secrets
techniques.summary: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.

techniques.name: Cached Domain Credentials
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

techniques.name: DCSync
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

techniques.name: Proc Filesystem
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or `/proc`.

techniques.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking.

techniques.name: Winlogon Helper DLL
techniques.summary: Winlogon.exe is a Windows component responsible for actions at logon/logoff as well as the secure attention sequence (SAS) triggered by Ctrl-Alt-Delete.

techniques.name: Data from Local System
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

techniques.name: Direct Volume Access
techniques.summary: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring.

techniques.name: System Service Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services.

techniques.name: Fallback Channels
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

techniques.name: Binary Padding
techniques.summary: Adversaries can use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware without affecting the functionality or behavior of the binary.

techniques.name: Application Window Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

techniques.name: Query Registry
techniques.summary: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

techniques.name: Port Monitors
techniques.summary: A port monitor can be set through the API call to set a DLL to be loaded at startup.

techniques.name: Rootkit
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components.

techniques.name: Accessibility Features
techniques.summary: Windows contains accessibility features that may be launched with a key combination before a user has logged in (for example, when the user is on the Windows logon screen).

techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems.

techniques.name: Internet Connection Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Wi-Fi Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Application Deployment Software
techniques.summary: Adversaries may deploy malicious software to systems within a network using application deployment systems employed by enterprise administrators.

techniques.name: Remote System Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system.

techniques.name: System Firmware
techniques.summary: The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) and The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) or Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) are examples of system firmware that operate as the software interface between the operating system and hardware of a computer.

techniques.name: Automated Exfiltration
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

techniques.name: Traffic Duplication
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure.

techniques.name: Remote Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).

techniques.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB).

techniques.name: Distributed Component Object Model
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM).

techniques.name: SSH
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH).

techniques.name: VNC
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

techniques.name: Windows Remote Management
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

techniques.name: Cloud Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities.

techniques.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted
techniques.summary: Data is encrypted before being exfiltrated in order to hide the information that is being exfiltrated from detection or to make the exfiltration less conspicuous upon inspection by a defender.

techniques.name: Shortcut Modification
techniques.summary: Shortcuts or symbolic links are ways of referencing other files or programs that will be opened or executed when the shortcut is clicked or executed by a system startup process.

techniques.name: Custom Cryptographic Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic.

techniques.name: Data from Removable Media
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

techniques.name: Multiband Communication
techniques.summary: **This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** Some adversaries may split communications between different protocols.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

techniques.name: Binary Padding
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware.

techniques.name: Software Packing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information.

techniques.name: Compile After Delivery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

techniques.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
techniques.summary: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.

techniques.name: HTML Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files.

techniques.name: Dynamic API Resolution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis.

techniques.name: Stripped Payloads
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information.

techniques.name: Embedded Payloads
techniques.summary: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses.

techniques.name: Command Obfuscation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection.

techniques.name: Fileless Storage
techniques.summary: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses.

techniques.name: LNK Icon Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files.

techniques.name: Encrypted/Encoded File
techniques.summary: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection.

techniques.name: Polymorphic Code
techniques.summary: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection.

techniques.name: Compression
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files.

techniques.name: Junk Code Insertion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware’s functionality.

techniques.name: SVG Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files.

techniques.name: Invisible Unicode
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text.

techniques.name: Windows Remote Management
techniques.summary: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).

techniques.name: Scheduled Transfer
techniques.summary: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals.

techniques.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
techniques.summary: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds.

techniques.name: Modify Existing Service
techniques.summary: Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Registry.

techniques.name: Standard Cryptographic Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may explicitly employ a known encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

techniques.name: System Owner/User Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

techniques.name: Path Interception
techniques.summary: **This technique has been deprecated.

techniques.name: Service Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute a binary, command, or script via a method that interacts with Windows services, such as the Service Control Manager.

techniques.name: Masquerading
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

techniques.name: Invalid Code Signature
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

techniques.name: Right-to-Left Override
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

techniques.name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
techniques.summary: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

techniques.name: Masquerade Task or Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign.

techniques.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
techniques.summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them.

techniques.name: Space after Filename
techniques.summary: Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file.

techniques.name: Double File Extension
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type.

techniques.name: Masquerade File Type
techniques.summary: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents.

techniques.name: Break Process Trees
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to evade process tree-based analysis by modifying executed malware's parent process ID (PPID).

techniques.name: Masquerade Account Name
techniques.summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign.

techniques.name: Overwrite Process Arguments
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process.

techniques.name: Browser Fingerprint
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.

techniques.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Logon Script (Windows)
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Login Hook
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon.

techniques.name: Network Logon Script
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: RC Scripts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system’s startup.

techniques.name: Startup Items
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: DLL Search Order Hijacking
techniques.summary: Windows systems use a common method to look for required DLLs to load into a program.

techniques.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

techniques.name: Network Sniffing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Change Default File Association
techniques.summary: When a file is opened, the default program used to open the file (also called the file association or handler) is checked.

techniques.name: Commonly Used Port
techniques.summary: **This technique has been deprecated.

techniques.name: File System Permissions Weakness
techniques.summary: Processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions.

techniques.name: Software Packing
techniques.summary: Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable.

techniques.name: Network Service Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: System Network Connections Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

techniques.name: New Service
techniques.summary: When operating systems boot up, they can start programs or applications called services that perform background system functions.

techniques.name: Shared Webroot
techniques.summary: **This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** Adversaries may add malicious content to an internally accessible website through an open network file share that contains the website's webroot or Web content directory and then browse to that content with a Web browser to cause the server to execute the malicious content.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

techniques.name: Exfiltration over USB
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: At (Linux)
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) utility to perform task scheduling for initial, recurring, or future execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: At

techniques.name: Cron

techniques.name: Launchd
techniques.summary: This technique is deprecated due to the inaccurate usage.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Systemd Timers
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse systemd timers to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Container Orchestration Job
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality provided by container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes to schedule deployment of containers configured to execute malicious code.

techniques.name: Indicator Blocking
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to block indicators or events typically captured by sensors from being gathered and analyzed.

techniques.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection

techniques.name: Portable Executable Injection

techniques.name: Thread Local Storage

techniques.name: Ptrace System Calls

techniques.name: Proc Memory

techniques.name: Extra Window Memory Injection

techniques.name: Input Capture

techniques.name: Keylogging

techniques.summary: Adversaries may install code on externally facing portals, such as a VPN login page, to capture and transmit credentials of users who attempt to log into the service.

techniques.name: Credential API Hooking

techniques.name: Process Discovery

techniques.name: Service Registry Permissions Weakness

techniques.name: User Execution
techniques.summary: An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution.

techniques.name: Malicious Link
techniques.summary: An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to gain execution.

techniques.name: Malicious File
techniques.summary: An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution.

techniques.name: Malicious Image
techniques.summary: Adversaries may rely on a user running a malicious image to facilitate execution.

techniques.name: Malicious Copy and Paste
techniques.summary: An adversary may rely upon a user copying and pasting code in order to gain execution.

techniques.name: Malicious Library
techniques.summary: Adversaries may rely on a user installing a malicious library to facilitate execution.

techniques.name: Traffic Signaling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control.

techniques.name: Port Knocking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use port knocking to hide open ports used for persistence or command and control.

techniques.name: Socket Filters
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attach filters to a network socket to monitor then activate backdoors used for persistence or command and control.

techniques.name: Sudo Caching
techniques.summary: The sudo command "allows a system administrator to delegate authority to give certain users (or groups of users) the ability to run some (or all) commands as root or another user while providing an audit trail of the commands and their arguments." Since sudo was made for the system administrator, it has some useful configuration features such as a timestamp_timeout that is the amount of time in minutes between instances of sudo before it will re-prompt for a password.

techniques.name: Rogue Domain Controller
techniques.summary: Adversaries may register a rogue Domain Controller to enable manipulation of Active Directory data.

techniques.name: Kerberoasting
techniques.summary: Service principal names (SPNs) are used to uniquely identify each instance of a Windows service.

techniques.name: Time Providers
techniques.summary: The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.

techniques.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exploit remote services to gain unauthorized access to internal systems once inside of a network.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Stealth
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities to evade detection by hiding activity, suppressing logging, or operating within trusted or unmonitored components.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to collect credentials.

techniques.name: Data from Information Repositories
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage information repositories to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Confluence
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage Confluence repositories to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Sharepoint
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the SharePoint repository as a source to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Code Repositories
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage code repositories to collect valuable information.

techniques.name: Customer Relationship Management Software
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage Customer Relationship Management (CRM) software to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Messaging Applications
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage chat and messaging applications, such as Microsoft Teams, Google Chat, and Slack, to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Databases
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage databases to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Credentials in Registry
techniques.summary: The Windows Registry stores configuration information that can be used by the system or other programs.

techniques.name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
techniques.summary: Loadable Kernel Modules (or LKMs) are pieces of code that can be loaded and unloaded into the kernel upon demand.

techniques.name: System Script Proxy Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use trusted scripts, often signed with certificates, to proxy the execution of malicious files.

techniques.name: PubPrn
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use PubPrn to proxy execution of malicious remote files.

techniques.name: SyncAppvPublishingServer
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs to proxy execution of malicious [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) commands.

techniques.name: Browser Information Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may enumerate information about browsers to learn more about compromised environments.

techniques.name: System Binary Proxy Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may bypass process and/or signature-based defenses by proxying execution of malicious content with signed, or otherwise trusted, binaries.

techniques.name: Compiled HTML File
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Compiled HTML files (.chm) to conceal malicious code.

techniques.name: Control Panel
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: CMSTP
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse CMSTP to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: InstallUtil
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use InstallUtil to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Mshta
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse mshta.exe to proxy execution of malicious .hta files and Javascript or VBScript through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Msiexec
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse msiexec.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: Odbcconf
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse odbcconf.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: Regsvcs/Regasm
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Regsvcs and Regasm to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Regsvr32
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Regsvr32.exe to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Rundll32
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse rundll32.exe to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Verclsid
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse verclsid.exe to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Mavinject
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse mavinject.exe to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: MMC
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse mmc.exe to proxy execution of malicious .msc files.

techniques.name: Electron Applications
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse components of the Electron framework to execute malicious code.

techniques.name: Remote Access Tools
techniques.summary: An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network.

techniques.name: IDE Tunneling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Integrated Development Environment (IDE) software with remote development features to establish an interactive command and control channel on target systems within a network.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Software
techniques.summary: An adversary may use legitimate desktop support software to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

techniques.name: Remote Access Hardware
techniques.summary: An adversary may use legitimate remote access hardware to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

techniques.name: XSL Script Processing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may bypass application control and obscure execution of code by embedding scripts inside XSL files.

techniques.name: Template Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify references in user document templates to conceal malicious code or force authentication attempts.

techniques.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Windows Permissions
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Linux and Mac Permissions
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Compiled HTML File
techniques.summary: Compiled HTML files (.chm) are commonly distributed as part of the Microsoft HTML Help system.

techniques.name: Execution Guardrails
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use execution guardrails to constrain execution or actions based on adversary supplied and environment specific conditions that are expected to be present on the target.

techniques.name: Environmental Keying
techniques.summary: Adversaries may environmentally key payloads or other features of malware to evade defenses and constraint execution to a specific target environment.

techniques.name: Mutual Exclusion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may constrain execution or actions based on the presence of a mutex associated with malware.

techniques.name: Domain Trust Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to gather information on domain trust relationships that may be used to identify lateral movement opportunities in Windows multi-domain/forest environments.

techniques.name: Domain Generation Algorithms
techniques.summary: Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains.

techniques.name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify the configuration settings of a domain or identity tenant to evade defenses and/or escalate privileges in centrally managed environments.

techniques.name: Group Policy Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to subvert the intended discretionary access controls for a domain, usually with the intention of escalating privileges on the domain.

techniques.name: Trust Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may add new domain trusts, modify the properties of existing domain trusts, or otherwise change the configuration of trust relationships between domains and tenants to evade defenses and/or elevate privileges.Trust details, such as whether or not user identities are federated, allow authentication and authorization properties to apply between domains or tenants for the purpose of accessing shared resources.

techniques.name: Data Destruction
techniques.summary: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.

techniques.name: Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify the lifecycle policies of a cloud storage bucket to destroy all objects stored within.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
techniques.summary: Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

techniques.name: Disk Structure Wipe
techniques.summary: Adversaries may corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on hard drive necessary to boot systems; targeting specific critical systems as well as a large number of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

techniques.name: Disk Content Wipe
techniques.summary: Adversaries may erase the contents of storage devices on specific systems as well as large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

techniques.name: Service Stop
techniques.summary: Adversaries may stop or disable services on a system to render those services unavailable to legitimate users.

techniques.name: Inhibit System Recovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may delete or remove built-in data and turn off services designed to aid in the recovery of a corrupted system to prevent recovery.

techniques.name: Defacement
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify visual content available internally or externally to an enterprise network, thus affecting the integrity of the original content.

techniques.name: Internal Defacement
techniques.summary: An adversary may deface systems internal to an organization in an attempt to intimidate or mislead users, thus discrediting the integrity of the systems.

techniques.name: External Defacement
techniques.summary: An adversary may deface systems external to an organization in an attempt to deliver messaging, intimidate, or otherwise mislead an organization or users.

techniques.name: Stored Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data at rest in order to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity.

techniques.name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may alter data en route to storage or other systems in order to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity.

techniques.name: Runtime Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify systems in order to manipulate the data as it is accessed and displayed to an end user.

techniques.name: Firmware Corruption
techniques.summary: Adversaries may overwrite or corrupt the flash memory contents of system BIOS or other firmware in devices attached to a system in order to render them inoperable or unable to boot, thus denying the availability to use the devices and/or the system.

techniques.name: Resource Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the resources of co-opted systems to complete resource-intensive tasks, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability.

techniques.name: Compute Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the compute resources of co-opted systems to complete resource-intensive tasks, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability.

techniques.name: Bandwidth Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the network bandwidth resources of co-opted systems to complete resource-intensive tasks, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability.

techniques.name: SMS Pumping
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage messaging services for SMS pumping, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability.

techniques.name: Cloud Service Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage compromised software-as-a-service (SaaS) applications to complete resource-intensive tasks, which may impact hosted service availability.

techniques.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments.

techniques.name: System Checks
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ various system checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments.

techniques.name: User Activity Based Checks
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments.

techniques.name: Time Based Checks
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, particularly those that attempt to manipulate time mechanisms to simulate longer elapses of time.

techniques.name: Network Denial of Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform Network Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of targeted resources to users.

techniques.name: Direct Network Flood
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target.

techniques.name: Reflection Amplification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by reflecting a high-volume of network traffic to a target.

techniques.name: Endpoint Denial of Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users.

techniques.name: OS Exhaustion Flood
techniques.summary: Adversaries may launch a denial of service (DoS) attack targeting an endpoint's operating system (OS).

techniques.name: Service Exhaustion Flood
techniques.summary: Adversaries may target the different network services provided by systems to conduct a denial of service (DoS).

techniques.name: Application Exhaustion Flood
techniques.summary: Adversaries may target resource intensive features of applications to cause a denial of service (DoS), denying availability to those applications.

techniques.name: Application or System Exploitation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities that can cause an application or system to crash and deny availability to users.

techniques.name: Compile After Delivery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

techniques.name: Systemd Service
techniques.summary: Systemd services can be used to establish persistence on a Linux system.

techniques.name: Parent PID Spoofing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may spoof the parent process identifier (PPID) of a new process to evade process-monitoring defenses or to elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
techniques.summary: Adversaries may acquire credentials from web browsers by reading files specific to the target browser.

techniques.name: PowerShell Profile
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges in certain situations by abusing [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1086) profiles.

techniques.name: Server Software Component
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse legitimate extensible development features of servers to establish persistent access to systems.

techniques.name: SQL Stored Procedures
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse SQL stored procedures to establish persistent access to systems.

techniques.name: Transport Agent
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft transport agents to establish persistent access to systems.

techniques.name: Web Shell
techniques.summary: Adversaries may backdoor web servers with web shells to establish persistent access to systems.

techniques.name: IIS Components
techniques.summary: Adversaries may install malicious components that run on Internet Information Services (IIS) web servers to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Terminal Services DLL
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse components of Terminal Services to enable persistent access to systems.

techniques.name: vSphere Installation Bundles
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors.

techniques.name: Web Session Cookie
techniques.summary: Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services.

techniques.name: Elevated Execution with Prompt
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to escalate privileges by prompting the user for credentials.

techniques.name: Software Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of software and software versions that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment.

techniques.name: Security Software Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment.

techniques.name: Backup Software Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of backup software or configurations that are installed on a system.

techniques.name: Emond
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Event Monitor Daemon (emond) to establish persistence by scheduling malicious commands to run on predictable event triggers.

techniques.name: Cloud Instance Metadata API
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access the Cloud Instance Metadata API to collect credentials and other sensitive data.

techniques.name: Implant Internal Image
techniques.summary: Adversaries may implant cloud or container images with malicious code to establish persistence after gaining access to an environment.

techniques.name: Cloud Service Discovery
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to enumerate the cloud services running on a system after gaining access.

techniques.name: Application Access Token
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems.

techniques.name: Steal Application Access Token
techniques.summary: Adversaries can steal application access tokens as a means of acquiring credentials to access remote systems and resources.

techniques.name: System Shutdown/Reboot
techniques.summary: Adversaries may shutdown/reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems.

techniques.name: Data from Cloud Storage
techniques.summary: Adversaries may access data from cloud storage.

techniques.name: Account Access Removal
techniques.summary: Adversaries may interrupt availability of system and network resources by inhibiting access to accounts utilized by legitimate users.

techniques.name: Internal Spearphishing
techniques.summary: After they already have access to accounts or systems within the environment, adversaries may use internal spearphishing to gain access to additional information or compromise other users within the same organization.

techniques.name: Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create cloud instances in unused geographic service regions in order to evade detection.

techniques.name: Revert Cloud Instance
techniques.summary: An adversary may revert changes made to a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

techniques.name: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data by transferring the data, including through sharing/syncing and creating backups of cloud environments, to another cloud account they control on the same service.

techniques.name: Cloud Service Dashboard
techniques.summary: An adversary may use a cloud service dashboard GUI with stolen credentials to gain useful information from an operational cloud environment, such as specific services, resources, and features.

techniques.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
techniques.summary: An adversary may steal web application or service session cookies and use them to gain access to web applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without needing credentials.

techniques.name: Pre-OS Boot
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Pre-OS Boot mechanisms as a way to establish persistence on a system.

techniques.name: System Firmware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify system firmware to persist on systems.The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) and The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) or Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) are examples of system firmware that operate as the software interface between the operating system and hardware of a computer.

techniques.name: Component Firmware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify component firmware to persist on systems.

techniques.name: Bootkit
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use bootkits to persist on systems.

techniques.name: ROMMONkit
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the ROM Monitor (ROMMON) by loading an unauthorized firmware with adversary code to provide persistent access and manipulate device behavior that is difficult to detect.

techniques.name: TFTP Boot
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse netbooting to load an unauthorized network device operating system from a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server.

techniques.name: Create or Modify System Process
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify system-level processes to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

techniques.name: Launch Agent
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify launch agents to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

techniques.name: Systemd Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify systemd services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

techniques.name: Windows Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

techniques.name: Launch Daemon
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify Launch Daemons to execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

techniques.name: Container Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify container or container cluster management tools that run as daemons, agents, or services on individual hosts.

techniques.name: Event Triggered Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges using system mechanisms that trigger execution based on specific events.

techniques.name: Change Default File Association
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by a file type association.

techniques.name: Screensaver
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by user inactivity.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by a Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription.

techniques.name: Unix Shell Configuration Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence through executing malicious commands triggered by a user’s shell.

techniques.name: Trap
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by an interrupt signal.

techniques.name: LC_LOAD_DYLIB Addition
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by the execution of tainted binaries.

techniques.name: Netsh Helper DLL
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by Netsh Helper DLLs.

techniques.name: Accessibility Features
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by accessibility features.

techniques.name: AppCert DLLs
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by AppCert DLLs loaded into processes.

techniques.name: AppInit DLLs
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by AppInit DLLs loaded into processes.

techniques.name: Application Shimming
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by application shims.

techniques.name: Image File Execution Options Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by Image File Execution Options (IFEO) debuggers.

techniques.name: PowerShell Profile
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by PowerShell profiles.

techniques.name: Emond
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by the Event Monitor Daemon (emond).

techniques.name: Component Object Model Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by hijacked references to Component Object Model (COM) objects.

techniques.name: Installer Packages
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by using an installer to trigger the execution of malicious content.

techniques.name: Udev Rules
techniques.summary: Adversaries may maintain persistence through executing malicious content triggered using udev rules.

techniques.name: Python Startup Hooks
techniques.summary: Adversaries may achieve persistence by leveraging Python’s startup mechanisms, including path configuration (`.pth`) files and the `sitecustomize.py` or `usercustomize.py` modules.

techniques.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may configure system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or logon to maintain persistence or gain higher-level privileges on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
techniques.summary: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key.

techniques.name: Authentication Package
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse authentication packages to execute DLLs when the system boots.

techniques.name: Time Providers
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots.

techniques.name: Winlogon Helper DLL
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse features of Winlogon to execute DLLs and/or executables when a user logs in.

techniques.name: Security Support Provider
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse security support providers (SSPs) to execute DLLs when the system boots.

techniques.name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify the kernel to automatically execute programs on system boot.

techniques.name: Re-opened Applications
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify plist files to automatically run an application when a user logs in.

techniques.name: LSASS Driver
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify or add LSASS drivers to obtain persistence on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Shortcut Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create or modify shortcuts that can execute a program during system boot or user login.

techniques.name: Port Monitors
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use port monitors to run an adversary supplied DLL during system boot for persistence or privilege escalation.

techniques.name: Plist Modification
techniques.summary: Adversaries can modify property list files (plist files) to execute their code as part of establishing persistence.

techniques.name: Print Processors
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse print processors to run malicious DLLs during system boot for persistence and/or privilege escalation.

techniques.name: XDG Autostart Entries
techniques.summary: Adversaries may add or modify XDG Autostart Entries to execute malicious programs or commands when a user’s desktop environment is loaded at login.

techniques.name: Active Setup
techniques.summary: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine.

techniques.name: Login Items
techniques.summary: Adversaries may add login items to execute upon user login to gain persistence or escalate privileges.

techniques.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
techniques.summary: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control privilege elevation to gain higher-level permissions.

techniques.name: Setuid and Setgid
techniques.summary: An adversary may abuse configurations where an application has the setuid or setgid bits set in order to get code running in a different (and possibly more privileged) user’s context.

techniques.name: Bypass User Account Control
techniques.summary: Adversaries may bypass UAC mechanisms to elevate process privileges on system.

techniques.name: Sudo and Sudo Caching
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform sudo caching and/or use the sudoers file to elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Elevated Execution with Prompt
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to escalate privileges by prompting the user for credentials.

techniques.name: Temporary Elevated Cloud Access
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse permission configurations that allow them to gain temporarily elevated access to cloud resources.

techniques.name: TCC Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries can manipulate or abuse the Transparency, Consent, & Control (TCC) service or database to grant malicious executables elevated permissions.

techniques.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.

techniques.name: Application Access Token
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems.

techniques.name: Pass the Hash
techniques.summary: Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls.

techniques.name: Pass the Ticket
techniques.summary: Adversaries may “pass the ticket” using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls.

techniques.name: Web Session Cookie
techniques.summary: Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services.

techniques.name: Unsecured Credentials
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials.

techniques.name: Credentials In Files
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search local file systems and remote file shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials.

techniques.name: Credentials in Registry
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search the Registry on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

techniques.name: Shell History
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search the command history on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

techniques.name: Private Keys
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search for private key certificate files on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

techniques.name: Cloud Instance Metadata API
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access the Cloud Instance Metadata API to collect credentials and other sensitive data.

techniques.name: Group Policy Preferences
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to find unsecured credentials in Group Policy Preferences (GPP).

techniques.name: Container API
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather credentials via APIs within a containers environment.

techniques.name: Chat Messages
techniques.summary: Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services.

techniques.name: Subvert Trust Controls
techniques.summary: Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs.
